builder_plan.scenario: Tool errors or unavailable services cause your agent to abandon recoverable tasks.
builder_plan.change: Inject repeatable tool failures and change only the recovery policy.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current retry and fallback behavior under the same injected failures.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Recovered tasks, duplicate side effects, retries, time to recovery, and total cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Idempotency Is Not Recovery: A Fault-Injection Study of Language-Model Agent Tool Actions
summary: The approach replaces naive retry-on-failure or assume-success handling of interrupted agent tool calls with a runtime combining an action ledger, target-side idempotency, post-crash reconciliation, and evidence sealing, distinguishing duplicate suppression from actual recovery. It costs roughly sevenfold throughput relative to a fail-open baseline plus the engineering complexity of maintaining the ledger, idempotent tool endpoints, and reconciliation logic. It can fail when evidence writes themselves are faulted (75/100 trials per platform left unresolved), when tools cannot be made idempotent, and results derive from a controlled benchmark with constructed cases and captured model responses rather than production traffic, so real-world fault coverage is unverified.
rationale: Any production agent that calls real tools can duplicate or lose side effects on interruption, and the paper's mechanisms (action ledger, idempotency keys, reconciliation, evidence sealing) are implementable on a single host without extra model capacity, but the sevenfold throughput cost means the full configuration should be validated against the reader's own latency and reliability requirements before adoption.
technique: Fault-tolerant agent tool-call runtime with ledger and reconciliation

claims.statement: The approach replaces naive retry-on-failure or assume-success handling of interrupted agent tool calls with a runtime combining an action ledger, target-side idempotency, post-crash reconciliation, and evidence sealing, distinguishing duplicate suppression from actual recovery. It costs roughly sevenfold throughput relative to a fail-open baseline plus the engineering complexity of maintaining the ledger, idempotent tool endpoints, and reconciliation logic. It can fail when evidence writes themselves are faulted (75/100 trials per platform left unresolved), when tools cannot be made idempotent, and results derive from a controlled benchmark with constructed cases and captured model responses rather than production traffic, so real-world fault coverage is unverified.

In 200 crash-and-replay pairs, the full configuration recorded 0/200 repeated side effects versus 117/200 for simpler baselines; a ledger ablation produced 170/170 orphaned effects and only 200/300 recovery successes versus 300/300; throughput was about one-seventh of the fail-open baseline.
